blocks.text: A pencil-thin single crystal of zinc, clamped at its ends and pulled by hand, stretches and flattens into a ribbon at a stress of less than one megapascal, far below what the strength of atomic bonds would suggest. Metals deform at stresses a thousand times lower than their bonds allow, because planes of atoms do not slide all at once: line defects called dislocations move across them one row at a time.

blocks.markdown: Plastic deformation in crystalline metals is **slip**: shear of one block of crystal over another along a crystallographic plane, carried by dislocation glide. A dislocation is a line defect: an extra half-plane of atoms ending in the crystal. When a shear stress acts on the slip plane, the dislocation moves one atomic row at a time and only the bonds along the dislocation line need to break, which is why the stress required is so small.

blocks.caption: Rigid sliding of whole planes (theoretical shear strength) would need a stress about 5000 times larger than the measured critical resolved shear stress; dislocation glide explains the difference.

blocks.title: Slip system and critical resolved shear stress
blocks.text: A **slip system** is a slip plane together with a slip direction in that plane. Slip occurs on the planes and in the directions of highest atomic density because the distance for each atom to move is shortest and the plane spacing is greatest. The **critical resolved shear stress** $\tau_{\text{CRSS}}$ is the shear stress, resolved on the slip plane in the slip direction, at which slip begins. It is a property of the material (for a given temperature and purity), not of the loading.

blocks.markdown: **Schmid's law.** A tensile force $F$ along the axis of a crystal of cross-sectional area $A$ gives a tensile stress $\sigma=F/A$. Let $\phi$ be the angle between the tensile axis and the **normal** to the slip plane, and $\lambda$ the angle between the tensile axis and the **slip direction**. The slip plane has area $A/\cos\phi$, and the component of $F$ along the slip direction is $F\cos\lambda$. Dividing gives the resolved shear stress.

blocks.caption: m is the Schmid factor; phi is the angle between the tensile axis and the slip-plane normal, lambda the angle between the axis and the slip direction. The product cos(phi)cos(lambda) never exceeds 0.5.

blocks.title: Resolved shear stress and yield of an aluminium crystal
blocks.prompt: An aluminium single crystal ($\tau_{\text{CRSS}}=0.8$ MPa, typical) is loaded in tension. The angle between the axis and the slip-plane normal is $\phi=50^\circ$ and the angle to the slip direction is $\lambda=45^\circ$. Find the Schmid factor and the tensile stress at which this system starts to slip.

steps.text: Slip begins when the resolved shear stress reaches the critical value: $m\sigma=\tau_{\text{CRSS}}$.

blocks.answer: Schmid factor 0.455; the crystal yields at about 1.76 MPa on this system.

blocks.markdown: **Which system slips first?** A crystal has several slip systems, each with its own $\phi$ and $\lambda$. The system with the **largest** Schmid factor reaches $\tau_{\text{CRSS}}$ first, so that is the system that operates. The largest possible value is $m=0.5$, when $\phi=\lambda=45^\circ$ (the axis, slip normal and slip direction lie in one plane). If the tensile axis is parallel to the slip direction ($\lambda=0$, so $\phi=90^\circ$) or perpendicular to the slip plane ($\phi=0$), then $m=0$ and that system cannot slip however large the stress.

blocks.title: Choosing the active system
blocks.prompt: A crystal has three slip systems with $(\phi,\lambda)$ of $(60^\circ,30^\circ)$, $(45^\circ,60^\circ)$ and $(75^\circ,40^\circ)$ with respect to the tensile axis. Taking $\tau_{\text{CRSS}}=1.0$ MPa, find the yield stress and the active system.

steps.text: Compute the Schmid factor of each system.
The first system has the largest factor, so it reaches the critical stress first and is the active system.
Yield stress from the active system.

blocks.answer: The first system, with m = 0.433, is active; the crystal yields at 2.31 MPa.

blocks.caption: Slip systems and ductility by crystal structure.

blocks.markdown: **FCC versus BCC.** FCC crystals have close-packed {111} planes and close-packed <110> directions, giving 4 planes times 3 directions = 12 systems, all with low and nearly temperature-independent $\tau_{\text{CRSS}}$. Hence FCC metals remain ductile down to very low temperatures. BCC crystals have no truly close-packed planes; slip occurs on several planes, giving many systems, but the lattice resistance (Peierls stress) is high and strongly dependent on temperature, so the yield stress climbs at low temperature and fracture can intervene. A polycrystal needs five independent systems to deform arbitrarily, which FCC and BCC supply but HCP at room temperature does not.

**Why a single crystal yields at $\tau_{\text{CRSS}}$.** A perfect crystal cannot flow plastically until a dislocation moves. Dislocations are mobile once the resolved shear stress on a slip system exceeds the lattice friction and the stress needed to overcome obstacles in the crystal; this value is $\tau_{\text{CRSS}}$. Below it the crystal deforms only elastically. Because the criterion is on the resolved shear stress, the **tensile** yield stress $\sigma_y=\tau_{\text{CRSS}}/m$ varies from crystal to crystal with orientation, even though $\tau_{\text{CRSS}}$ is constant for the material. A crystal at $m=0.5$ is the softest, and one with $m$ near zero is the hardest.

blocks.title: Orientation changes the tensile yield stress, not the CRSS
blocks.text: Two identical crystals can have very different tensile yield stresses simply because they are cut at different angles. Compute the resolved shear stress on every available system, find the highest Schmid factor, and divide $\tau_{\text{CRSS}}$ by that value. The result for a polycrystal is an average over many grains.

blocks.title: Check the angle geometry
blocks.text: The angles $\phi$ and $\lambda$ are measured from the tensile axis to two directions which are themselves at $90^\circ$ (the plane normal and the slip direction lie at right angles), so $\phi+\lambda\ge90^\circ$ and $\cos\phi\cos\lambda\le0.5$. A pair of angles that violates this cannot describe a real slip system.

points: Slip proceeds by dislocation glide on close-packed planes and directions, which is why real metals yield at stresses thousands of times below the theoretical shear strength.

Schmid's law: $\tau_R=\sigma\cos\phi\cos\lambda$; slip begins on the system with the largest Schmid factor when $\tau_R$ reaches $\tau_{\text{CRSS}}$, so $\sigma_y=\tau_{\text{CRSS}}/m$ and $m\le0.5$.
FCC has 12 close-packed slip systems and stays ductile at low temperature, BCC has many systems with a temperature-sensitive lattice resistance, and HCP has few at room temperature.

questions.stem: A single crystal of a metal is loaded in tension and begins to deform plastically. Which statement correctly explains the onset of yielding?

options.text: Slip starts when the tensile stress reaches a material constant that is independent of orientation
Slip starts when the normal stress on the slip plane reaches the theoretical bond strength
Slip starts when the resolved shear stress on the most favourably oriented slip system reaches the critical value
Slip starts on all slip systems at once when the applied stress exceeds the shear modulus divided by 100

questions.correctOptionText: Slip starts when the resolved shear stress on the most favourably oriented slip system reaches the critical value

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: the tensile yield stress varies with orientation; the constant is the resolved shear stress.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: normal stress on the plane does not drive slip, and theoretical bond strength is far too high.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: yielding begins when the resolved shear stress on the best-oriented system reaches $\tau_{\text{CRSS}}$, which is a material property.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: slip begins first on the single most favoured system, and the stress is a thousand times lower than G/100.

questions.explanation: Slip is driven by shear, and the shear stress available on each system depends on orientation through the Schmid factor. The first system to reach $\tau_{\text{CRSS}}$ operates, giving a tensile yield stress of $\tau_{\text{CRSS}}/m$.

questions.stem: How many slip systems does an FCC crystal have, and what are they?

options.text: 12: four {111} planes with three <110> directions on each
8: four {111} planes with two <110> directions on each
3: one basal plane with three <11-20> directions
48: six {110} planes with eight <111> directions on each

questions.correctOptionText: 12: four {111} planes with three <110> directions on each

distractorRationale.a: Correct: 4 close-packed planes multiplied by 3 close-packed directions on each plane.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: each {111} plane contains three, not two, close-packed directions.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this describes the HCP basal plane at room temperature.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this is the count for BCC crystals when {110}, {112} and {123} planes are all included, not for FCC.

questions.explanation: The close-packed planes in FCC are the four {111} planes, and each contains three close-packed <110> directions, so there are $4\times3=12$ systems. This large number of low-resistance systems underlies the high ductility of FCC metals.

questions.stem: A single crystal has its tensile axis at $\phi=60^\circ$ to the slip-plane normal and $\lambda=50^\circ$ to the slip direction. What is the Schmid factor for this system?

options.text: About 0.64
About 0.50
About 1.14
About 0.32

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: this is $\cos50^\circ$ alone and ignores the factor from the plane normal.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: 0.50 is the maximum possible value, reached only at 45 degrees for both angles.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this adds the two cosines, but the Schmid factor is their product and can never exceed 0.5.

questions.explanation: The Schmid factor is the product $m=\cos\phi\cos\lambda=\cos60^\circ\times\cos50^\circ=0.5\times0.643=0.32$. It is less than 0.5, as it must be, so the crystal needs a tensile stress about three times the critical resolved shear stress to slip on this system.

questions.stem: A tensile stress of 12 MPa is applied to a single crystal. For one slip system the angle between the axis and the slip-plane normal is $\phi=48^\circ$ and the angle between the axis and the slip direction is $\lambda=52^\circ$. Calculate the resolved shear stress on this system, in MPa.
questions.explanation: By Schmid's law $\tau_R=\sigma\cos\phi\cos\lambda=12\times\cos48^\circ\times\cos52^\circ=12\times0.6691\times0.6157=4.94$ MPa. This is the stress that drives dislocation glide on that system.

questions.stem: A zinc single crystal has a critical resolved shear stress of 0.18 MPa (typical) on its basal slip system. It is pulled in tension with the axis at $\phi=70^\circ$ to the basal-plane normal and $\lambda=30^\circ$ to the slip direction. Calculate the tensile stress at which it yields, in MPa.
questions.explanation: The Schmid factor is $\cos70^\circ\cos30^\circ=0.3420\times0.8660=0.2962$. Yield occurs when $m\sigma=\tau_{\text{CRSS}}$, so $\sigma_y=0.18/0.2962=0.608$ MPa.

questions.stem: Which loading orientation of a single crystal makes the resolved shear stress on a given slip system largest for a given tensile stress?

options.text: The tensile axis parallel to the slip direction
The tensile axis at 45 degrees both to the slip-plane normal and to the slip direction
The tensile axis perpendicular to the slip plane
The tensile axis at 60 degrees to the slip-plane normal and 90 degrees to the slip direction

questions.correctOptionText: The tensile axis at 45 degrees both to the slip-plane normal and to the slip direction

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: if the axis lies along the slip direction, the angle to the plane normal is 90 degrees and the factor is zero.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: $\cos45^\circ\cos45^\circ=0.5$, the maximum possible Schmid factor.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: with the axis along the plane normal there is no shear on the plane and the factor is zero.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: a right angle to the slip direction gives zero resolved force along it, so the factor is zero.

questions.explanation: Resolved shear stress is $\sigma\cos\phi\cos\lambda$, and the product of cosines is largest when both angles are 45 degrees, where it equals 0.5. Any orientation where either angle is 90 degrees gives zero shear on that system.

questions.stem: Copper (FCC) remains ductile at liquid-nitrogen temperature, whereas a ferritic iron (BCC) can fracture in a brittle way at the same temperature. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: FCC metals have fewer slip systems, so dislocations can concentrate on one plane
BCC metals have close-packed planes that become blocked when the temperature falls
Copper has a larger Schmid factor than iron at every temperature
FCC slip systems have a low lattice resistance that depends little on temperature, whereas in BCC the resistance to dislocation motion rises steeply at low temperature

questions.correctOptionText: FCC slip systems have a low lattice resistance that depends little on temperature, whereas in BCC the resistance to dislocation motion rises steeply at low temperature

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: FCC has more, not fewer, slip systems (12), all on close-packed planes.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: BCC has no truly close-packed planes; the temperature sensitivity comes from the lattice friction.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the Schmid factor depends only on orientation and not on the material or temperature.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: BCC yield stress rises sharply as temperature falls and can exceed the fracture stress.

questions.explanation: FCC slip occurs on close-packed planes with a low and nearly temperature-independent critical resolved shear stress. In BCC the lattice resistance to dislocation motion rises steeply at low temperature, raising the yield stress above the stress needed for cleavage, which produces a ductile-to-brittle transition.

questions.stem: Crystal A, with Schmid factor 0.47 on its operating system, yields at a tensile stress of 2.1 MPa. A second crystal B of the same metal yields at a tensile stress of 3.9 MPa. Find the Schmid factor of the operating system in crystal B. Give a dimensionless number.
questions.explanation: The critical resolved shear stress is the same in both crystals, and from crystal A it is $\tau_{\text{CRSS}}=0.47\times2.1=0.987$ MPa. For crystal B, $m_B=\tau_{\text{CRSS}}/\sigma_y=0.987/3.9=0.253$.

questions.stem: Compare the slip systems of FCC and BCC crystals and explain how they account for the difference in the ductility of the two structures at low temperature. State the number of systems in FCC.
markingGuide: FCC: close-packed {111} planes and <110> directions, 4 planes x 3 directions = 12 systems
BCC: no close-packed plane; slip on {110}, {112}, {123} planes in <111> directions (48 systems in total)
FCC has low critical resolved shear stress that depends little on temperature
In BCC the lattice resistance (Peierls stress) increases steeply as temperature falls
So BCC metals show a ductile-to-brittle transition while FCC metals stay ductile at low temperature
May mention that HCP has few systems at room temperature and limited ductility
questions.explanation: Ductility depends on how easily dislocations can move on enough systems. Close-packed FCC planes keep the lattice resistance low at all temperatures, whereas BCC lattice resistance rises as temperature falls and fracture can intervene.

questions.stem: Derive Schmid's law for a single crystal in uniaxial tension, and use it to calculate the tensile yield stress of an aluminium crystal with $\tau_{\text{CRSS}}=0.8$ MPa for which $\phi=55^\circ$ and $\lambda=40^\circ$. Explain why this stress depends on orientation although $\tau_{\text{CRSS}}$ does not.
markingGuide: Tensile force F on area A gives $\sigma=F/A$
Slip plane area is $A/\cos\phi$ and the force component along the slip direction is $F\cos\lambda$
Explains that $\tau_{\text{CRSS}}$ is a material property, whereas $m$ depends on orientation, so tensile yield stress varies from crystal to crystal
questions.explanation: Resolving the tensile force onto the slip plane and along the slip direction gives the Schmid factor. Because slip is controlled by the resolved shear stress, the tensile yield stress is the material constant divided by an orientation-dependent factor.
